newsitem.title: USA: Trial under way in landmark Florida tobacco lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: Trial under way in landmark Florida tobacco lawsuit.

text.p: Florida's landmark billion-dollar lawsuit against the tobacco industry to recover the cost of treating sick smokers went to trial on Friday with a vow from Gov. Lawton Chiles to reap "tobacco justice."
The heralded lawsuit, closely watched by financial markets and legal scholars, is one of 40 filed against tobacco companies by U.S. state governments and the first to go to trial.

Florida is seeking to recover some $1 billion used to treat Medicaid recipients suffering from smoking-related illnesses. The lawsuit also accuses tobacco companies of racketeering, opening the door to recovery of billions of dollars in past profits.

Outside the Palm Beach County courthouse, Chiles said 1994 revisions his government enacted to the state's Medicaid Third Party Liability Act that specifically targeted the industry would level the playing field with Big Tobacco.
"I think that because of that, we're going to see a verdict that's going to give us tobacco justice," he said.
Florida filed the lawsuit in in Feb. 1995, the fourth state to do so, but it is the first to bring its case before a jury. Mississippi, the first state to file, has already settled its suit.

Legal analysts have said a verdict for Florida could establish a legal precedent that tobacco companies are responsible for the damage caused by their products. At trial, Florida will argue tobacco companies conspired to mislead the public about the dangers of cigarette smoking.
The prominence of the trial was evident from its opening moments. When Chiles and Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth walked into the packed jury room, a murmur swept through the crowd.
"It's an important day," one prospective juror said.
Palm Beach Circuit Judge Harold Cohen introduced both Butterworth and Chiles, who is the only named plaintiff in the lawsuit against the major tobacco companies and two industry groups.

The judge gave the pool of prospective jurors, from which six jurors and nine alternates will be selected, a brief overview of the case, saying that the state alleged the tobacco companies were "negligent and that they manufactured and distributed a defective product."

The prospective jurors were given an 11-page questionnaire and sent home. They will be brought back in groups over the next month. Testimony is expected to begin in early September and the trial could last until January, Cohen said.

Butterworth, who said the trial would provide the American public with its first chance to learn "the full truth about ... what they (tobacco companies) have been hiding for the past 40 years," declined to say whether the state was actively negotiating a settlement with the industry.
"The lines of communication are open but nobody's on our side of the phone right now," he said.
The two sides hammered away at each other in pre-trial motions, during which Cohen issued critical rulings that damaged both the state and the industry.
In one ruling, he barred the state collecting future damages, removing some $16 billion in possible payouts.
But in a critical ruling just two days ago, Cohen stripped the industry of one of its primary defences -- that Medicaid recipients knew the dangers of smoking.

That ruling prompted tobacco giant Philip Morris to issue a statement late Thursday, just hours before jury selection began, saying the state had made it "nearly impossible" for the industry to get a fair trial.
On Friday, industry attorneys said they were ready. "We're glad to get the process started," R.J. Reynolds lawyer Bob Weber said.
